Dog Aging Project · Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine
Scaling Scientific Discovery in the Dog Aging Project
How Texas A&M and the Dog Aging Project used VetRec to turn thousands of unstructured veterinary records into research-ready data — and helped clear the way for a study of 100,000+ records.
processed in initial study

Historically, DAP researchers and graduate assistants extracted these data points by hand — opening each record, finding the relevant values, and typing them into a structured database. At an estimated 15 to 30 minutes per record, that approach is the bottleneck between data collection and discovery.
Any extraction approach had to produce variables clean and reliable enough to support primary scientific research, not just operational reporting.
Data security and provenance
Records had to be processed through a controlled, project-specific pipeline that protected participant data and preserved a clear chain of custody.

In partnership with VetRec, the DAP team conducted an initial study to evaluate whether AI-assisted extraction could replace manual chart review for a defined set of clinical variables. The study focused on longitudinal body weight — a deceptively simple variable that, in practice, requires reading every visit note to capture each measurement, its date, and its unit.
Secure, project-specific ingestion
VetRec ingested the source PDFs through a secure transfer location dedicated to the Dog Aging Project, isolating the data from any unrelated workflow.
The team and VetRec built an extraction template focused on the project's specific clinical variables, starting with longitudinal body weight — value, date, and unit per measurement.
From a 59-record proof point to a 100,000+ record collaboration
Extraction time per record collapsed from 15–30 minutes of manual chart review to seconds of automated processing.
The study will be presented at the 2026 ACVIM Forum on Thursday, June 11 in a talk titled "Using Artificial Intelligence for Scalable Data Extraction from Medical Records in the Dog Aging Project."
On the strength of these findings, the collaboration is expanding to process more than 100,000 records, with a peer-reviewed publication planned as the next milestone.
